q: Broad, ribbon-like, aseptate hyphae branching at wide (90-degree) angles on KOH mount of necrotic sinus tissue in a diabetic ketoacidosis patient is characteristic of which fungal genus?
why: Correct — Mucorales show broad aseptate hyphae with wide-angle branching, linked to DKA
Aspergillus shows narrow, septate hyphae at acute angles, morphologically distinct
Candida shows budding yeast with pseudohyphae
Histoplasma is seen as small intracellular yeast forms, not hyphae
exp: Mucorales (Mucor, Rhizopus, Rhizomucor) show broad, ribbon-like, aseptate hyphae with wide-angle (near 90-degree) branching — contrasted with Aspergillus's narrow, septate, acute-angle (45-degree) branching hyphae; Mucorales cause rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis, strongly associated with uncontrolled diabetes/DKA.

subject: Microbiology
q: A gardener develops a nodule at a thorn-prick site followed by a chain of similar nodules tracking proximally along the lymphatics ('sporotrichoid spread'). Which dimorphic fungus is the most likely cause?
why: Correct — Sporothrix schenckii causes classic thorn-prick sporotrichoid lymphangitis
Blastomyces causes primarily pulmonary infection with occasional cutaneous lesions, not the classic thorn-prick chain
Coccidioides causes primarily pulmonary disease, endemic to the Americas
Paracoccidioides causes South American pulmonary/mucocutaneous disease, distinct presentation
exp: Sporothrix schenckii ('rose gardener's disease') is a dimorphic fungus inoculated through minor skin trauma (thorns, splinters), producing a primary nodule followed by ascending nodular lymphangitis along the draining lymphatics — a distinctive 'sporotrichoid' pattern also seen with some atypical mycobacteria (M. marinum) and nocardia.

subject: Microbiology
q: Antigenic shift in influenza A virus, responsible for pandemics, occurs due to:
opts: Point mutation in the hemagglutinin gene during replication
Homologous recombination within one strain's RNA genome
Post-translational glycosylation of the neuraminidase protein
Reassortment of genome segments between two co-infecting strains
why: Point mutation describes antigenic drift (seasonal epidemics), not shift
Influenza does not undergo classic homologous recombination
Glycosylation changes are not the mechanism of antigenic shift
Correct - reassortment of the 8-segment genome produces a novel subtype capable of pandemic spread
exp: Antigenic shift results from reassortment of the influenza virus's 8-segment RNA genome when two different strains co-infect a host cell (e.g. pig as mixing vessel), producing a novel subtype capable of pandemics, unlike drift's gradual point mutations causing seasonal epidemics.

subject: Microbiology
q: Branching septate hyphae seen on 10% KOH mount of skin scrapings from an annular, scaly, itchy plaque are characteristic of: Image described: ring-shaped erythematous plaque with central clearing and an active raised border.
why: Correct - dermatophytes show septate branching hyphae on KOH
Candida shows budding yeast with pseudohyphae, not this pattern
Malassezia shows a spaghetti-and-meatballs pattern of hyphae plus spores
Sporothrix is dimorphic, shown as cigar-shaped yeast in tissue
exp: KOH mount showing branching septate hyphae from an annular scaly plaque is the classic bedside diagnostic finding for dermatophytosis (tinea) - a quick, cheap test every JMO should be able to perform and read.

subject: Microbiology
q: Fourth-generation HIV ELISA reduces the diagnostic window period compared to third-generation assays because it additionally detects:
opts: IgM antibodies to HIV envelope glycoproteins
why: RNA PCR is a separate NAT test, not part of the ELISA itself
Correct - detecting p24 antigen along with antibody catches acute infection earlier
Proviral DNA detection is not part of routine 4th-gen ELISA
IgM antibody detection is the advance of the third-generation sandwich ELISA, not the fourth; the fourth generation adds p24 antigen on top of IgM/IgG
exp: Fourth-generation HIV ELISA combines p24 antigen and antibody detection, narrowing the window period because p24 antigen appears in blood before antibody seroconversion - relevant to post-exposure testing timelines per NACO guidelines.

subject: Microbiology
q: For diagnosis of Wuchereria bancrofti infection by peripheral blood smear, blood should ideally be collected at:
why: Morning collection misses the peak count
Midday is the nadir of circulating microfilariae
Correct - nocturnal periodicity peaks in this window
Periodicity is real and clinically important for sample timing
exp: Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae exhibit nocturnal periodicity, concentrating in peripheral blood at night (classically 10 PM-2 AM) while sequestering in pulmonary capillaries by day - this dictates that diagnostic blood smears must be collected at night.

subject: Microbiology
q: Which culture medium, containing egg, glycerol, and malachite green, is classically used for the isolation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
why: Bordet-Gengou medium is the classical selective medium for Bordetella pertussis
TCBS agar is selective for Vibrio cholerae, giving yellow sucrose-fermenting colonies
Loeffler's serum slope is used for Corynebacterium diphtheriae and metachromatic granules
Correct — LJ medium is the classical TB culture medium
exp: Lowenstein-Jensen medium is an egg-based selective medium containing glycerol (favouring M. tuberculosis over M. bovis) and malachite green (inhibits contaminating growth), remaining the classical gold-standard solid medium for mycobacterial culture, though slower (2-8 weeks) than liquid systems like BACTEC/MGIT.

subject: Microbiology
q: A child from a rural endemic area develops transient dry cough, wheeze, and peripheral eosinophilia about 1-2 weeks after presumed ingestion of soil-contaminated food, followed about 2 months later by passage of a large roundworm in the stool. The pulmonary phase is best explained by:
opts: Direct larval invasion of the myocardium
Hypersensitivity to migrating Strongyloides filariform larvae
Loeffler syndrome from pulmonary migration of Ascaris larvae
why: Ascaris larvae migrate through the lungs, not the myocardium, during their life cycle
Strongyloides can cause a similar picture, but the large roundworm in stool specifically fits Ascaris
Correct — classic Loeffler syndrome from Ascaris larval migration
The eosinophilic, self-limiting nature argues against a bacterial pneumonia
exp: After ingestion of Ascaris eggs, larvae hatch, penetrate the gut wall, and migrate via the portal circulation to the lungs, breaking into alveoli and being swallowed to mature in the intestine; this pulmonary transit provokes a transient hypersensitivity pneumonitis with cough, wheeze, and marked eosinophilia known as Loeffler syndrome, occurring about 1-2 weeks after egg ingestion — roughly 2 months before adult worms or eggs appear in stool (total egg-to-adult cycle ~60-75 days).

subject: Microbiology
q: Japanese encephalitis virus is transmitted by Culex tritaeniorhynchus mosquitoes, with which animal acting as the key amplifying host in the transmission cycle?
why: Cattle are not the key amplifying host for JE virus
Correct — pigs are the classic JE amplifying host
Dogs are not implicated in the JE transmission cycle
Bats are reservoirs for other viruses like Nipah/rabies, not JE
exp: Japanese encephalitis virus is maintained in a zoonotic cycle between Culex mosquitoes and vertebrate amplifying hosts, with pigs as the principal amplifying host (high-titre viraemia without significant illness) and ardeid wading birds as reservoirs; humans and horses are incidental dead-end hosts.

subject: Microbiology
q: A motile, flagellated, pear-shaped organism is seen on a wet mount of vaginal discharge from a woman with a frothy, malodorous discharge and a strawberry cervix on speculum examination. The organism and its first-line treatment are:
why: Candida causes a thick curd-like discharge with budding yeast/pseudohyphae, not a motile flagellate
Gardnerella (bacterial vaginosis) shows clue cells and a fishy whiff-test odour, not a motile flagellated organism
The organism identification is correct but azithromycin is not standard first-line treatment for trichomoniasis
Correct — Trichomonas vaginalis with metronidazole as first-line therapy
exp: Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated protozoan STI causing a frothy, malodorous discharge with vulvovaginal irritation and, in a minority, the characteristic strawberry cervix; diagnosis is by seeing motile trophozoites on saline wet mount, and first-line treatment is oral metronidazole with simultaneous partner treatment.

subject: Microbiology
q: A patient treated for acute vivax malaria completes chloroquine therapy but relapses 3 months later. Which parasite stage, and which drug for its eradication, explains this relapse?
opts: Hypnozoites in the liver; primaquine (after checking G6PD status)
Sporozoites in mosquito salivary glands; mefloquine
why: Gametocytes are the sexual, transmissible stage, not the cause of relapse
Blood-stage merozoites cause the acute attack, already treated, not the cause of late relapse
Correct, dormant hepatic hypnozoites reactivate months later
Sporozoites are the mosquito-to-human infective stage, irrelevant to relapse
exp: Only P. vivax and P. ovale form hypnozoites, explaining their unique relapsing pattern; P. falciparum and P. malariae never relapse this way. Primaquine is the only widely available hypnozoiticidal drug, but mandatory G6PD screening before use is a frequently tested safety point.

subject: Microbiology
q: A patient from a sheep-rearing rural area presents with a slowly enlarging cystic liver lesion. Serology confirms Echinococcus granulosus infection. What is the definitive host of this parasite, in whose intestine the adult tapeworm resides?
why: Sheep are the intermediate host, harboring larval hydatid cysts, not the adult worm
Humans are an accidental intermediate host, not the definitive host
Correct, dogs harbor the adult tapeworm and shed eggs in feces
Cattle can be an intermediate host in some cycles but are not the definitive host
exp: The Echinococcus granulosus life cycle is dog (definitive host, adult worm) - sheep (natural intermediate host, larval hydatid cyst) - with humans as an accidental intermediate host who develop hydatid cysts after ingesting eggs from food/water contaminated by dog feces; percutaneous aspiration (PAIR) of cysts carries anaphylaxis risk from cyst fluid leakage.

subject: Microbiology
q: Measles (rubeola) infection is characterized histopathologically by which multinucleated giant cell finding in lymphoid tissue?
why: Wrong — Negri bodies are cytoplasmic inclusions in rabies-infected neurons (Purkinje cells, hippocampus).
Wrong — owl's eye inclusions are the classic CMV intranuclear inclusion.
Wrong — Councilman bodies are apoptotic hepatocytes seen in yellow fever/viral hepatitis.
Correct — pathognomonic multinucleated giant cells with inclusions in lymphoid tissue in measles.
exp: Measles produces Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells — multinucleated syncytial giant cells with eosinophilic intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions — found in lymphoid tissue (tonsils, lymph nodes, appendix) during the prodromal and early rash phase, and considered pathognomonic for measles infection.

subject: Microbiology
q: Image described: CT chest in a neutropenic patient showing a pulmonary nodule surrounded by a ground-glass halo. In invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, this finding reflects early hemorrhagic infarction and is termed?
why: Wrong — the air crescent sign is a later finding, appearing as the necrotic center retracts, not the early hemorrhagic phase.
Wrong — tree-in-bud pattern suggests small airway/bronchiolar infection, not an angioinvasive fungal nodule.
Wrong — crazy paving is classic for pulmonary alveolar proteinosis or some viral pneumonias, not aspergillosis's angioinvasive pattern.
Correct — the halo sign is the early hemorrhagic infarct/ground-glass rim around the fungal nodule seen in angioinvasive early disease.
exp: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis CT findings evolve over time: early, the halo sign (ground-glass hemorrhagic rim around a nodule from fungal angioinvasion); later, as neutrophils recover, the air crescent sign (crescent of air as the necrotic center retracts). Aspergillus shows septate hyphae with acute-angle (about 45 degree) branching on histopathology, distinguishing it from Mucor's broad aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching.

subject: Microbiology
q: Wilson-Blair (bismuth sulfite) medium, on which Salmonella Typhi produces characteristic jet-black colonies, exploits which property of the organism?
why: Correct — S. Typhi reduces sulfite and produces H2S, which reacts with iron/bismuth salts in the medium to form black, metallic-sheen colonies.
Lactose fermentation is assessed on media like MacConkey agar and is not the basis of black colony formation here.
Urease activity helps identify organisms like Proteus or Klebsiella, not Salmonella typing on this medium.
Indole production differentiates E. coli from Klebsiella and is unrelated to this medium's colony colour reaction.
exp: Wilson-Blair (bismuth sulfite) medium is a selective medium for isolating Salmonella Typhi from stool or environmental samples — H2S production by the organism reacts with iron salts in the medium to give characteristic jet-black colonies with a metallic sheen.

subject: Microbiology
q: Which culture medium is classically used for the primary isolation of Bordetella pertussis from a nasopharyngeal swab?
why: Loeffler's serum slope is for Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
TCBS agar is the selective medium for Vibrio cholerae.
Correct — the classical selective medium for Bordetella pertussis.
Lowenstein-Jensen medium is for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
exp: Bordet-Gengou (potato-glycerol-blood) agar is the classical selective medium for Bordetella pertussis; charcoal-based Regan-Lowe medium is more commonly used now but Bordet-Gengou remains the traditional exam answer.

subject: Microbiology
q: Which insect vector transmits Leishmania donovani, the cause of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) in the Indian subcontinent?
why: Culex quinquefasciatus transmits Wuchereria bancrofti (filariasis).
Anopheles culicifacies is a principal malaria vector in India.
Correct — sandfly vector for visceral leishmaniasis.
Aedes aegypti transmits dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever.
exp: Phlebotomus argentipes, the sandfly, is the proven vector for Leishmania donovani transmission in the Bihar-Jharkhand-UP-West Bengal kala-azar belt targeted by India's elimination programme.

subject: Microbiology
q: A 45-year-old spelunker (cave explorer) from the Gangetic plain presents with fever, weight loss, and hepatosplenomegaly. Bone marrow biopsy shows small oval yeast forms clustered within macrophages, each surrounded by a clear halo. Which fungus is most likely responsible?
why: Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast seen extracellularly with an India-ink halo, not intracellular in macrophages, and is linked to pigeon droppings, not caves
Correct — intracellular yeast in macrophages after cave/bat exposure is the classic histoplasmosis picture
Blastomyces shows broad-based budding yeast and is a North American endemic mycosis, not cave-associated
Coccidioides forms spherules containing endospores in tissue, not small intracellular yeast, and is linked to desert soil, not caves
exp: Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that exists as small intracellular budding yeast within macrophages at body temperature; classic exposure is bat/bird droppings in caves (spelunker's disease), with endemic pockets along India's Gangetic river belt.

subject: Microbiology
q: Which intestinal nematode is unique among human helminths in its ability to complete its entire life cycle within a single host through an autoinfective cycle, allowing infection to persist for decades and to hyperinfect immunosuppressed patients?
why: Ascaris eggs must mature in soil before becoming infective - no autoinfective cycle
Ancylostoma eggs must mature in soil into filariform larvae before skin penetration - no autoinfection
Enterobius has perianal-to-oral retro-infection via scratching but not a true internal autoinfective larval cycle
Correct - Strongyloides larvae can reinvade the same host internally, enabling lifelong persistence and hyperinfection
exp: Strongyloides stercoralis rhabditiform larvae can transform into infective filariform larvae within the gut/perianal skin and reinvade the same host (autoinfection), so untreated infection can persist lifelong; in immunosuppressed patients (steroids, HTLV-1, transplant) this can accelerate into fatal hyperinfection/disseminated strongyloidiasis - hence screening and treating with ivermectin before immunosuppression in at-risk patients.

subject: Microbiology
q: A 6-year-old girl has intense perianal itching that worsens at night, disturbing her sleep. Her mother notices small white thread-like worms around the anus in the morning. Which is the most reliable method to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: Stool routine examination for ova and cysts
Perianal adhesive (cellophane) tape test performed first thing in the morning before bathing or defecation
why: Stool O&C is often negative since eggs are deposited perianally, not passed in stool in useful numbers
Correct — captures eggs before they are washed off or hatch
Eosinophilia is nonspecific and often minimal in enterobiasis since the worm does not invade tissue
Duodenal aspirate is used for Giardia/Strongyloides, not pinworm
exp: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) female migrates out at night to lay eggs on perianal skin; eggs are rarely passed in stool, so routine stool exam is often negative. The tape test (Graham's/Scotch-tape test, or NIH swab) applied to perianal skin each morning before washing captures eggs for microscopy — the standard confirmatory test.

subject: Microbiology
q: Which simple bedside test distinguishes Streptococcus pneumoniae from viridans streptococci on culture?
why: Coagulase test differentiates Staph aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci, not relevant here
Correct — optochin sensitivity is diagnostic for S. pneumoniae
Catalase test differentiates staphylococci (positive) from streptococci (negative), not pneumococcus from viridans strep
Bacitracin sensitivity distinguishes Group A strep (S. pyogenes) from other beta-hemolytic streptococci
exp: Streptococcus pneumoniae is optochin-sensitive and bile-soluble, whereas viridans streptococci are optochin-resistant — the standard laboratory method to differentiate these two alpha-hemolytic streptococci on culture.

subject: Microbiology
q: Formation of germ tubes after incubation in serum at 37 degrees C for 2-3 hours is a rapid presumptive identification test for which fungus?
why: Cryptococcus neoformans is identified by an India ink halo/capsule, not germ tubes
Aspergillus fumigatus is a mould identified by septate hyphae with acute-angle branching, not a yeast germ tube test
Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus identified by morphology change with temperature, not the germ tube test
Correct - germ tube formation in serum within 2-3 hours is diagnostic for C. albicans
exp: The germ tube test (Reynolds-Braude phenomenon) - filamentous outgrowths forming from yeast cells within 2-3 hours of incubation in serum at 37 degrees C - is a rapid presumptive test that distinguishes Candida albicans from other Candida species, which are germ-tube negative.

subject: Microbiology
q: NS1 antigen testing for dengue fever is most useful during which window of illness, being detectable before IgM antibodies appear?
opts: Only in the convalescent phase after day 15
Only during a second (secondary) dengue infection
why: Correct - NS1 is an early-phase marker, present before seroconversion.
By 10-14 days NS1 positivity has usually waned as the antibody response takes over; it is not the optimal window.
Convalescent-phase diagnosis relies on IgG/IgM serology, not NS1, which has largely cleared by then.
NS1 sensitivity is actually lower in secondary infection due to antigen-antibody immune complexing, so it is not exclusive to secondary infections.
exp: NS1 is a dengue viral glycoprotein secreted into the blood from the onset of viraemia, detectable from day 1 and reliably positive through roughly day 9 of illness - well before IgM antibodies typically rise around day 5 and become the mainstay of diagnosis thereafter. The exact positivity window varies slightly by assay.

subject: Microbiology
q: Which selective culture medium shows yellow colonies for Vibrio cholerae due to sucrose fermentation?
why: MacConkey agar is a general selective medium for gram-negative enteric bacilli, not specific for Vibrio
Correct - TCBS plus sucrose fermentation gives yellow colonies for V. cholerae
Loeffler's serum slope is used to enhance metachromatic granule formation in Corynebacterium diphtheriae
Chocolate agar is an enriched medium for fastidious organisms like Haemophilus and Neisseria
exp: TCBS agar is the selective and differential medium for Vibrio species; V. cholerae ferments sucrose and appears as yellow colonies, while non-sucrose fermenters like V. parahaemolyticus appear green - a high-yield medium-organism pairing.

subject: Microbiology
q: Persistent infection with which two HPV genotypes carries the highest risk of progression to cervical cancer?
why: HPV 6 and 11 are low-risk types causing genital warts (condyloma acuminata), not cancer.
HPV 31 and 33 are also high-risk types but account for a much smaller proportion of cervical cancers than 16 and 18.
HPV 42 and 44 are low-risk, non-oncogenic types.
Correct - HPV 16 and 18 together account for roughly 70 percent of cervical cancers worldwide and are the genotypes targeted by HPV vaccines.
exp: High-risk HPV genotypes 16 and 18 account for roughly 70 percent of cervical cancers worldwide, with HPV 16 predominantly causing squamous cell carcinoma and HPV 18 more associated with adenocarcinoma. Low-risk types 6 and 11 cause genital warts, not cancer. India's national HPV vaccination programme targets these high-risk genotypes.

subject: Microbiology
q: During the window period of acute Hepatitis B infection, when HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared, which serological marker is the only one detectable?
why: HBeAg, a marker of active replication, typically clears before HBsAg and is gone before the window period
Anti-HBe appears with e-antigen seroconversion but is not the reliable sole marker of the window period
Correct — IgM anti-HBc is the sole detectable marker that bridges the Hepatitis B window period
HBV DNA may be detectable but is not the classic serological teaching marker used for this window
exp: The Hepatitis B window period is the gap between disappearance of HBsAg and appearance of anti-HBs, during which IgM anti-HBc is the only detectable serological marker — essential for diagnosing acute HBV infection in a patient who would otherwise test falsely negative on an HBsAg/anti-HBs panel alone.

subject: Microbiology
q: The satellite phenomenon around a Staphylococcus aureus streak on blood agar helps identify which gram-negative organism requiring both X and V factors?
why: Correct — H. influenzae needs factor X and V, supplied by Staph aureus haemolysis products on blood agar
Bordetella pertussis needs Bordet-Gengou or charcoal-blood agar, not X/V supplementation
N. meningitidis grows on chocolate agar/Thayer-Martin medium, not X/V dependent
M. catarrhalis grows on ordinary blood or chocolate agar without an X/V requirement
exp: H. influenzae requires factor X (haemin) and factor V (NAD) for growth; on blood agar these are released by a Staphylococcus aureus streak, producing larger satellite colonies of H. influenzae closer to the staph streak — useful when chocolate agar is unavailable.

subject: Microbiology
q: A gravid tapeworm proglottid shows 15-20 lateral uterine branches on microscopy. Which species does this identify?
why: Correct - Taenia saginata proglottids show 15-20 lateral uterine branches, more numerous than T. solium.
Taenia solium has fewer (7-13) uterine branches, the classic contrast pair.
Diphyllobothrium latum has a rosette-shaped uterus, not a branching one.
Hymenolepis nana proglottids do not show this branching uterine pattern.
exp: Counting lateral uterine branches on a gravid proglottid differentiates the two human Taenia species: Taenia saginata has 15-20 branches (beef tapeworm), Taenia solium has 7-13 (pork tapeworm) - the classic morphological discriminator on stool/proglottid examination.

subject: Microbiology
q: Stool microscopy showing trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells is diagnostic of infection with which organism?
why: Correct — erythrophagocytosis is a diagnostic feature of invasive E. histolytica.
Giardia lamblia trophozoites are pear-shaped, binucleate and flagellated, with no RBC ingestion.
Balantidium coli is a large ciliate causing dysentery, but this feature is not its diagnostic hallmark.
Entamoeba coli is a non-pathogenic commensal and, by definition, never contains ingested RBCs.
exp: Erythrophagocytosis (RBC-laden trophozoites) on stool microscopy is specific and diagnostic for invasive Entamoeba histolytica, and is the key feature distinguishing it from the non-pathogenic commensal Entamoeba coli.

subject: Microbiology
q: Which mosquito genus transmits Wuchereria bancrofti, whose microfilariae show nocturnal periodicity in peripheral blood?
why: Anopheles transmits malaria (Plasmodium species), not filariasis
Correct — Culex quinquefasciatus is the principal vector of bancroftian filariasis across most of India
Aedes transmits dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever, not filariasis
Mansonia transmits Brugia malayi, the other filarial species causing lymphatic filariasis in India, not W. bancrofti
exp: Wuchereria bancrofti (over 90 percent of Indian filariasis cases) is transmitted by Culex quinquefasciatus; microfilariae show nocturnal periodicity matching the vector's night-biting habit. Brugia malayi, by contrast, is transmitted by Mansonia.

subject: Microbiology
q: Image described: India ink preparation of CSF from an HIV-positive patient showing round, budding yeast cells surrounded by a wide, clear halo. Which organism does this represent?
exp: Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast; its polysaccharide capsule excludes the India ink particles, producing the characteristic clear halo, a classic rapid test for cryptococcal meningitis in immunocompromised patients. Cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) latex agglutination is more sensitive for confirmation.

subject: Microbiology
q: Primary maternal CMV infection in pregnancy causes the most severe fetal brain injury when infection occurs in which trimester?
opts: Risk of severe damage is equal across all trimesters
exp: Two opposite gradients get conflated here. Transmission rate rises with gestational age (lowest in the first trimester, highest in the third), but severity of damage if transmission happens is greatest with first-trimester infection, because that window coincides with active neuronal proliferation and migration. The question asks about severity, not the chance of transmission.

subject: Microbiology
q: Which motility pattern is characteristic of Giardia lamblia trophozoites on a fresh stool wet mount?
exp: Giardia lamblia trophozoites show a characteristic 'falling leaf' motility produced by the beating of their four pairs of flagella, best appreciated on a fresh wet mount of watery diarrheal stool. The binucleate, pear-shaped trophozoite and the oval, quadrinucleate cyst are the two forms to recognize.

subject: Microbiology
q: Negri bodies, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions seen in neurons, are diagnostic of infection with which virus?
exp: Negri bodies are cytoplasmic, round-to-oval eosinophilic inclusions found classically in Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and hippocampal pyramidal neurons in rabies encephalitis, remaining a key diagnostic clue at autopsy. Herpes simplex encephalitis instead shows Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions, and JC virus (PML) shows oligodendrocyte nuclear inclusions.

subject: Microbiology
q: Which morphological form seen on a peripheral blood smear is pathognomonic for Plasmodium falciparum infection?
opts: Schuffner's dots with an enlarged RBC
exp: Crescent (banana)-shaped gametocytes on thick/thin smear are unique to P. falciparum among human malaria parasites. Schuffner's dots with an enlarged host RBC instead point to P. vivax/ovale.

subject: Microbiology
q: Large cells showing intranuclear owl's eye inclusion bodies on histopathology are characteristic of infection with which virus?
exp: Enlarged cells with a basophilic intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo (owl's eye) are pathognomonic for cytomegalovirus, seen in lung, colon, retina, and placenta, classically in immunocompromised hosts and congenital CMV infection.

subject: Microbiology
q: Metachromatic (Babes-Ernst) granules seen on Albert staining are a characteristic microscopic feature of which organism?
exp: Corynebacterium diphtheriae shows club-shaped pleomorphic bacilli arranged in Chinese-letter or cuneiform patterns, with intracellular metachromatic (volutin/Babes-Ernst) granules that stain differently from the cell body on Albert's or Neisser's stain — a rapid presumptive bedside clue used before culture confirmation on Loeffler's serum slope or tellurite medium.

subject: Microbiology
q: A stool sample from a suspected cholera outbreak must be transported to a district lab 6 hours away. Which transport medium is appropriate?
exp: Cary-Blair is the transport medium of choice for Vibrio cholerae and most enteric pathogens - alkaline pH suits Vibrio, and it holds organisms viable for days at ambient temperature without refrigeration.

subject: Microbiology
q: Which stain is used to demonstrate Cryptosporidium oocysts in a stool sample?
exp: Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora and Isospora oocysts are acid-fast and are demonstrated by modified (cold) Ziehl-Neelsen. India ink is for the Cryptococcus capsule - a common distractor pairing.

subject: Microbiology
q: A Gram-positive bacillus isolated from the CSF of a neonate shows characteristic tumbling motility in broth at 25 degrees C but is non-motile at 37 degrees C. The likely organism is:
exp: Temperature-dependent tumbling motility (present at 25 C, absent at 37 C) is the classic identifier for Listeria. It also grows at refrigeration temperature, which is the basis of cold enrichment and of its link with stored dairy foods.

subject: Microbiology
q: Which intestinal cestode is unique in being able to complete its entire life cycle within a single human host without requiring an intermediate host?
why: Correct — unique autoinfective, single-host life cycle.
Taenia solium requires a pig (or accidental human) intermediate host for the larval stage.
Diphyllobothrium latum requires two intermediate hosts, a copepod and a fish.
Echinococcus granulosus requires a dog definitive host with sheep or human as intermediate host.
exp: Hymenolepis nana (dwarf tapeworm) can complete egg-to-adult development entirely within one human gut via autoinfection, enabling direct human-to-human transmission without an obligatory intermediate host — this explains its status as the most common cestode infection worldwide, especially in crowded or institutional settings.

subject: Microbiology
q: The most common causative fungal organism for otomycosis (fungal otitis externa) reported in Indian clinical series is:
why: Candida albicans is a common but secondary cause of otomycosis in most Indian series.
Correct — A. niger is the leading isolate.
Aspergillus fumigatus causes otomycosis less frequently than A. niger.
Malassezia furfur causes pityriasis versicolor/seborrheic dermatitis, not typically otomycosis.
exp: Aspergillus niger is consistently the leading isolate in Indian otomycosis series, followed by Candida species, producing itching and characteristic black/grey debris with a 'wet newspaper' appearance on otoscopy. Treatment is aural toilet plus topical antifungal drops.

subject: Microbiology
q: Congenital microcephaly with intracranial calcifications, following a mild maternal febrile illness with rash in an Aedes-endemic area, is most classically linked to infection with which virus?
why: Chikungunya causes fever with severe arthralgia, not a recognized congenital microcephaly syndrome.
Dengue causes hemorrhagic fever/thrombocytopenia without an established congenital microcephaly link.
Correct — Zika is specifically linked to congenital microcephaly.
Japanese encephalitis causes pig-amplified encephalitis in children, not typically congenital microcephaly from mild maternal infection.
exp: Zika virus (Aedes aegypti-borne flavivirus) causes congenital Zika syndrome — microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, and ocular abnormalities — following maternal infection, especially in the first trimester, even though the maternal illness itself is usually mild.

subject: Microbiology
q: Deficiency of which complement component most classically predisposes to recurrent severe infections with encapsulated pyogenic bacteria, rather than specifically Neisserial infections?
why: C5-C9 deficiency classically causes recurrent Neisserial infections, not the broad pyogenic pattern asked here.
C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, not recurrent pyogenic infection.
Factor D deficiency is an alternative-pathway defect with milder, less classic infection susceptibility.
Correct — C3 deficiency causes the severe generalized pyogenic infection pattern.
exp: C3 sits at the convergence point of the classical, alternative, and lectin pathways, so its deficiency severely impairs opsonization and predisposes to recurrent severe infections with encapsulated pyogenic organisms — in contrast, terminal complement (C5-C9/MAC) deficiency specifically predisposes to recurrent Neisserial infections.

subject: Microbiology
q: Romana's sign (unilateral painless periorbital edema) occurring after a triatomine ('kissing bug') bite is characteristic of infection with which parasite?
why: Correct — Romana's sign is diagnostic of acute Chagas disease.
Trypanosoma brucei causes African sleeping sickness via tsetse fly, unrelated to Romana's sign.
Leishmania donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis via sandfly bite, not triatomine transmission.
Toxoplasma gondii is transmitted via cat feces or undercooked meat, unrelated to triatomine bugs.
exp: Romana's sign is the classic finding of acute Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis) caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted when triatomine bug feces are rubbed into the bite wound or conjunctiva. Chronic Chagas disease later causes cardiomyopathy and megacolon/megaesophagus.

subject: Microbiology
q: A farmer presents with a chronically swollen foot with multiple discharging sinuses draining black grains after a thorn-prick injury. Which organism is the most common cause of this eumycotic mycetoma in India?
why: Nocardia brasiliensis is a bacterial cause of actinomycetoma with paler grains, not eumycetoma.
Correct — the leading fungal cause of black-grain Madura foot in India.
Actinomyces israelii causes actinomycosis, a bacterial mycetoma cause, not classic black-grain Madura foot.
Sporothrix schenckii causes sporotrichosis with lymphocutaneous nodules, not mycetoma.
exp: Madurella mycetomatis is the leading fungal (eumycotic) cause of 'Madura foot' in India, producing the classic triad of tumefaction, multiple sinuses, and grain discharge — black grains for eumycetoma, versus the paler grains of bacterial actinomycetoma (Nocardia/Actinomyces).

subject: Microbiology
q: Discrete, umbilicated, pearly dome-shaped skin papules caused by a poxvirus, common in children and sexually transmitted in adults, are characteristic of infection with:
why: HPV causes warts and cervical dysplasia, not umbilicated poxvirus papules.
HSV causes painful grouped vesicles, not painless umbilicated papules.
Correct — the classic umbilicated poxvirus lesion.
VZV causes vesicular chickenpox or dermatomal zoster, not umbilicated papules.
exp: Molluscum contagiosum virus, a Poxviridae member, produces umbilicated papules with a central caseous core (Henderson-Patterson bodies on histology). It spreads by direct skin contact or fomites in children and as an STI in sexually active adults, with more extensive lesions in immunosuppressed patients.

subject: Microbiology
q: A child with recurrent pyogenic infections, partial oculocutaneous albinism, and giant granules in neutrophils on peripheral smear most likely has which immunodeficiency?
why: Chronic granulomatous disease presents with recurrent catalase-positive organism infections and an abnormal NBT/DHR test, without albinism or giant granules.
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency presents with delayed umbilical cord separation and absent pus formation, without albinism.
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome presents with eczema, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections, without albinism or giant granules.
Correct — giant granules plus partial albinism is diagnostic of Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
exp: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder (LYST gene) causing giant lysosomal granules in neutrophils and melanocytes, leading to partial albinism, recurrent pyogenic infections from impaired chemotaxis/degranulation, peripheral neuropathy, and a later accelerated lymphoproliferative phase.
